overview: This two-page file documents the postwar clearance of wartime mines from Japanese waters under the Allied occupation. A despatch from the Office of the United States Political Adviser for Japan transmits a Far East Command press release reporting that Japanese minesweepers, supervised by the U.S. Navy and financed by the Japanese government, had cleared several major ports without any ships being damaged in swept channels. The release describes the use of approximately 1,500 personnel, 50 vessels, and specialized “guinea-pig ships,” while noting that magnetic mines continued to present some danger and that operations were expected to last until August 1950.

subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting press release on mine sweeping
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards a Far East Command press release concerning progress in clearing mines from Japanese waters.
subfiles.summary: The Acting Political Adviser transmits a September 22 press release entitled “Mine Sweeping Program Makes Headway.” The despatch highlights the absence of ship damage in cleared channels, names six cleared ports, and explains that Japanese personnel perform the work under U.S. Navy supervision at the Japanese government’s expense.

subfiles.title: Far East Command press release, “Mine Sweeping Program Makes Headway”
subfiles.from: Public Information Office, General Headquarters, Far East Command
subfiles.about: The release reports the scope, methods, achievements, and remaining hazards of the occupation-era Japanese minesweeping program.
subfiles.summary: Vice Admiral Russell S. Berkey reports that no ships had struck or been damaged by mines in channels swept since the occupation began. The program, conducted by the Japanese Maritime Safety Bureau under U.S. Navy supervision, employed nearly 1,500 personnel and 50 vessels and was expected to continue through August 1950. Specialized guinea-pig ships tested unswept and newly cleared waters, while operations proceeded in the Seto Inland Sea and Shimonoseki Strait after the clearance of several major ports. Although acoustic and pressure mines were thought to pose little remaining danger, magnetic mines remained a concern, with approximately 3,450 already rendered ineffective.

interest: The file offers a compact quantitative account of one of the occupation’s less visible but essential reconstruction projects, including personnel and vessel totals, estimates of mines laid, and the number of magnetic mines neutralized. Its discussion of “guinea-pig ships” is especially useful for understanding contemporary methods of detecting pressure and acoustic mines. The documents also illuminate the division of responsibility between Japanese personnel, the Japanese government, and U.S. naval authorities during the occupation.
